title: This Is the Best Gaming Phone, If You Can Accept the Compromises
gist: Wired gives the Nubia Redmagic 12 Pro gaming phone a 6/10: it pairs the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 with heavy cooling and an 8,400-mAh battery for class-leading Android performance, but a price hike to $949 makes its weak camera processing, bloatware, and two-year platform update commitment harder to accept.

insights.claim: Nubia, like other phone makers in 2026, delivered only minimal iterative improvements on the Redmagic 12 Pro while raising the starting price significantly to $949.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Industry-wide smartphone price hikes with minimal upgrades suggest component cost pressure and weaker value propositions; watch unit demand elasticity.
insights.quote: Sadly, Nubia has followed every other phone manufacturer this year, offering minimal iterative improvements while jacking up the price significantly.
insights.locator: Sadly, Nubia has followed every other phone

insights.claim: The Redmagic 12 Pro costs $949 for 12 GB RAM/256 GB storage, $1,049 for 16 GB/512 GB, and $1,199 for the 1-TB model.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Price ladder benchmarks gaming-phone ASPs against flagship Android competitors.
insights.locator: For buyers in the US, check

insights.claim: The Redmagic series has historically been a clear bargain for gamers wanting the best chipset, but at $949 its camera, software and update compromises become harder to justify.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Value-brand positioning erodes when prices converge with mainstream flagships like the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
insights.locator: Sadly, Nubia has followed every other phone

insights.claim: A Google Pixel 11 Pro XL can be bought on sale for the same price as the Redmagic 12 Pro, offering a more well-rounded phone.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Discounting of Pixel flagships pressures niche Android brands at the same price point.
insights.locator: Our best Android phones guide includes

insights.claim: The Redmagic 12 Pro uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 plus Redmagic's own RedCore R5 chip, topping Android benchmark charts above Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra and rivaling the iPhone 18 Pro.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Qualcomm's top-bin silicon keeps Android performance at parity with Apple; a positive for Qualcomm's premium mix.
insights.locator: Perhaps the biggest enticement is Qualcomm’s

insights.claim: The same Snapdragon chipset will roll into more phones soon, mostly with better cameras and longer software support but at higher prices, such as the forthcoming Motorola Signature 27 at $1,600.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: A $1,600 Motorola flagship signals rising premium Android ASPs; watch Qualcomm design wins across OEMs.
insights.locator: Our best Android phones guide includes

insights.claim: Nubia combines a fan, vapor chamber and new dual-loop liquid cooling so the phone sustains top-tier performance through an hour of demanding gaming, though with some fan noise and thermal throttling.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Active thermal management is a differentiator for sustained mobile performance as chips get hotter.
insights.locator: I had no issues playing Asphalt

insights.claim: The Redmagic 12 Pro's Gravity X game space includes an embedded Steam emulator that lets users log into Steam and potentially play PC games, though not all titles work.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: PC-game emulation on phones extends Steam's reach to mobile and blurs PC/mobile gaming boundaries.
insights.locator: Nubia includes a dedicated game space

insights.claim: The phone's 6.85-inch OLED reaches a 185-Hz refresh rate but only a handful of games such as PUBG Mobile support it, so most play is capped at 120 Hz.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Spec-sheet refresh rates outpace game-developer support, limiting their real-world value.

insights.claim: An 8,400-mAh battery lets the Redmagic 12 Pro last a full day of heavy gaming and potentially two days with careful use, with up to 80-watt wired or wireless charging but no Qi2 magnet support.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Large silicon-carbon-era batteries are becoming a key spec battleground for Android OEMs.
insights.locator: To keep you gaming for longer

insights.claim: Nubia lacks Google's image-processing expertise, so a camera system that looks similar on paper produces far worse photos, with off colors, poor mixed-light handling, and noisy or oversharpened shots.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Computational photography remains a moat for Google and Apple that hardware specs alone cannot replicate.
insights.quote: Nubia lacks Google’s expertise in this space, so a camera system that sounds similar on paper produces far worse photos in reality.
insights.locator: The real problem with the 12 Pro’s camera

insights.claim: The Redmagic 12 Pro's flat, bump-free design leaves no room for a telephoto lens, limiting zoom to 2X via cropping.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Design trade-offs for gaming ergonomics cost camera capability, narrowing the phone's addressable market.
insights.locator: To get top-notch performance at this price

insights.claim: Nubia promises only two years of platform updates and three years of security updates in the US (five in the UK), well below mainstream Android flagships, and ships Redmagic OS 12 on Android 17 with junk bloatware.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Short update commitments reduce device lifespan and resale value, a structural weakness of smaller Chinese OEMs in the US.
insights.locator: Another big turnoff with the 12 Pro

insights.claim: Chinese phone manufacturers continue to imitate Apple design language such as Liquid Glass in their Android skins.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Apple's UI direction continues to set the template copied by Android OEMs.
insights.locator: Another big turnoff with the 12 Pro

insights.claim: The Redmagic 12 Pro works with T-Mobile and its MVNOs but may not work with some other US carriers, and lacks eSIM support, requiring a physical SIM card.
insights.speaker: Simon Hill
insights.so_what: Carrier band and eSIM gaps cap the US addressable market for Chinese OEMs selling direct.
